claim.text: Common mistake: many people think crossing a double white line briefly is allowed. That is wrong.

correction.text: Crossing a double white line to enter or leave the express lane is prohibited; use dotted-line access points only.

answer.text: Only at dotted-line access points, because crossing the double white line is prohibited.

prompt.text: Where may you move into or out of the express lane, and what line must you respect?

rationale.text: Double white lines bar crossing, so lawful movement happens only where dotted access points appear.

lines.text: Flex lanes can reverse direction daily.
Freeways reward steady spacing and lawful choices.

narration.text: Welcome to freeway, flex and express lane rules for Utah roads. Flex lanes may reverse direction by time of day, so you check the overhead signal before entering. On the freeway you keep at least two seconds of following distance and lengthen the gap when conditions worsen. A left-lane driver approached from behind must move safely right so faster traffic can pass, since lingering can draw a citation for impeding. Together these habits keep fast traffic orderly and predictable for every driver around you.

lines.text: Keep at least two seconds behind.
Move right for faster traffic behind.

narration.text: Freeway spacing protects your stopping margin at higher speeds. Keep at least two seconds of following distance on the freeway and lengthen the gap when rain, snow, darkness or heavy traffic worsen conditions. A left-lane driver approached from behind must move safely right so faster traffic can pass. Lingering in the left lane blocks flow and can draw a citation for impeding. Watch the mirror, signal, check the blind spot, then slide right when it is safe.

lines.text: Emergency lane is for emergencies only.
Runaway ramps allow emergency stops only.

narration.text: Some freeway actions are never allowed because they endanger everyone at speed. U-turns on the freeway are prohibited, as is driving or stopping for passengers in the emergency lane outside the solid white line. That outer lane is reserved for true emergencies. Similarly, runaway-vehicle ramps are for emergency stops only, and stopping, standing or parking on or in the path of one is prohibited. Keep moving with traffic and use proper exits and parking areas instead.

lines.text: Two or more occupants ride free.
Motorcycles, buses and decal vehicles included.
Cross only at dotted access points.

narration.text: Express lanes on I-15 reward shared travel, but the entry rule traps hurried drivers. They are free for vehicles with two or more occupants, plus motorcycles, buses and registered clean-fuel decal vehicles. Crossing a double white line to enter or leave the express lane is prohibited. You may enter or exit only at dotted-line access points. Occupancy decides whether you may ride free, while dotted markings decide where you may cross. Do not mix those two ideas.

lines.text: Meters release one vehicle per green.
Obey only when meter sign lit.

narration.text: Ramps and special interchanges meter your entry for safety and flow. Ramp meters show alternating red and green and generally release one vehicle per green. You obey only when the meter-on sign is lit. At a single-point interchange, a U-turn from the off-ramp that re-enters the freeway is allowed only when facing a green arrow, and you finish once started. stopping midway would block crossing traffic, so commit and clear the intersection smoothly.

lines.text: Recall where express entry is lawful.
Double white means do not cross.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: where may you move into or out of the express lane, and what line must you respect. Think about the difference between who may ride free and where movement is allowed. The rule bars crossing the double white line at any point. Lawful entry and exit happen only at dotted-line access points, where markings open the lane for merging.

lines.text: Check signals before each lane choice.
Hold spacing and share left lane.

narration.text: You now have the core freeway routine for this section. Check the overhead signal before entering a flex lane. Keep at least two seconds behind and move right for faster traffic. Keep express use to qualified vehicles and dotted-line access points only. Carry those checks into intersections and markings next, where scanning and yielding build on the same careful lane discipline.

why_how.text: Flex lanes reverse by time of day, so the overhead signal tells whether your direction may use the lane right now.
Double white lines bar crossing to keep fast express traffic separated, so dotted access points create the only safe merge gaps.

reasoning.text: The driver qualifies by occupancy, but still needs a lawful entry point, so waiting for dotted striping satisfies both rules.

result.text: The driver merges at the dotted access point and stays out of the double-white section.

scenario.text: A driver with two passengers wants the I-15 express lane and approaches a double-white section before a dotted opening.

memory_support.text: Slow scan assume nothing; stop behind yield at any crosswalk; first there goes first.

claim.text: Myth, a misconception: a crosswalk needs paint before you must yield. That is not true.

correction.text: Stop behind the stop line or crosswalk and grant passage to anyone in or entering any crosswalk, marked or not.

answer.text: Yes, stop behind the line and grant passage because the duty applies to marked or unmarked crosswalks.

prompt.text: Must you grant passage to a walker entering an unmarked crosswalk at a signal?

rationale.text: The rule protects anyone in or entering any crosswalk, so paint does not remove the duty to stop behind and yield.

lines.text: Slow and scan each intersection fully.

narration.text: Intersections ask you to manage many users at once with care. At every intersection slow, scan for controls, cross traffic, walkers, riders and sight blocks, and never assume others will yield. That scanning habit sets up every later choice about stopping, markings, signals and priority. Keep speed low enough to see clearly and respond smoothly when someone else misses a sign or signal.

lines.text: Stop fully behind lines and walks.
Yield at any crosswalk marked or not.

narration.text: Stopping position shapes safety for walkers and cross traffic. Stop fully behind signs, signals, walks or stop lines. When queued, leave room to see the rear tires of the vehicle ahead, which preserves an escape margin. Stop behind the stop line or crosswalk at signs and signals and grant passage to anyone in or entering any crosswalk, marked or not. Stay behind the line so walkers can pass without stepping into traffic.

lines.text: Broken yellow may allow safe passing.
Five hundred feet, unless last car is farther.

narration.text: Center markings tell you when sharing space is lawful. Broken yellow center lines permit passing when safe, while solid lines and double-center lines restrict or bar passing as marked. Before entering a shared center left-turn lane, check mirrors, signal left and check the left blind spot. Do not enter more than five hundred feet before turning unless the last car is farther than five hundred feet from the intersection. Keep the shared lane available for opposing turners. Default limits absent signs or hazards are 20 near schools during arrival and dismissal, 25 in business and residential areas, and 55 on major highways as posted.

lines.text: Steady yellow warns red is near.
Yield to prior arrival and right tie.

narration.text: Signals and priority connect stopping to going. Steady yellow means the signal is about to turn red, while flashing yellow means slow, proceed with care and be ready to stop. A flashing yellow arrow permits the turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and walkers, who hold the green. Grant the way to the vehicle already in the intersection, to oncoming traffic on a left turn, to the driver on the right at a tied four-way stop, and to road traffic when leaving a drive. Reduce speed where sight or control is reduced.

Here is a quick check: must you grant passage to a walker entering an unmarked crosswalk at a signal. Picture approaching a signal with no painted lines and a walker stepping toward the crossing. Remember where to stop and who holds passage at any crosswalk, marked or not. Decide what your full stop and yielding action should be.

Close this unit by linking signs and special crossings. Warning signs are generally diamond-shaped yellow with black symbols, while guide signs are square or rectangular green, brown or blue. Work-zone signs are diamond or rectangular orange with black legends, and speeding fines in work zones are doubled. Cross rail tracks promptly without stopping on them, and handle roundabouts by slowing, yielding inside, entering when clear and exiting at the wanted street.

why_how.text: Slowing and scanning matters because controls, cross traffic, walkers and sight blocks all meet at intersections and others may not yield.
Yielding at any crosswalk protects walkers who may lawfully cross without paint, so stopping behind preserves their path.

reasoning.text: The driver slows, scans, stops behind the line and waits because a walker entering any crosswalk holds passage.

result.text: The driver grants passage and proceeds only after the crosswalk is clear.

scenario.text: A driver nears a signalized crossing with an unmarked crosswalk where a walker steps toward the road.

memory_support.text: Green clear yellow caution; red waits officer rules.

claim.text: Trap, many people think green always means go and a red light always controls over an officer. That is wrong.

correction.text: Green means go only if clear, and an officer directing traffic overrides any signal indication.

answer.text: Stop and wait, allow right on red after stop unless barred, honor red arrows, and obey the officer over the light.

prompt.text: At a red light with an officer waving you through, must you stay stopped or follow the officer?

rationale.text: Red requires stop and wait, but officer directions override signals, so the officer order governs movement.

narration.text: This spine ties lane, interchange and signal rules into one routine. Flex-lane use follows the overhead signal, with green arrow open and red cross closed. Express lanes need qualifying occupancy, and double white line crossing is barred except at dotted access points. Notice how each special lane pairs permission with a clear visual cue. Learning those pairs first makes entry, exit and yielding choices much easier.

Freeway discipline blends spacing with courteous merging. Keep the following gap and avoid turnarounds, emergency-lane driving and ramp reversal. A left-lane vehicle approached from behind must move right to avoid impeding. Use the acceleration lane to match speed, exit early and steady, and pass a metered ramp one vehicle per green. Matching speed, holding space and yielding the left lane keep high-speed merges safe and lawful.

Special interchanges channel unusual movements through signals and lane guides. Runaway ramps are emergency-only with no stopping, while the single-point off-ramp U-turn is allowed on green arrow and must finish once started, never stopping mid-crossing. Continuous-flow, diverging-diamond and thru-U-turn layouts each redirect left turns, so follow staged signals and lane guides. Trust the arrows and pavement guides rather than improvising a direct turn.

Intersection and marking basics support lawful speed. Approach slow and scan, stop behind the line, look left-right-left, cross without lane change, then merge right. Yellow divides opposing flow while white divides same-direction flow, with stops behind the line and yield in crosswalks and limited shared-center entry. The basic law is reasonable-and-prudent speed with posted defaults by area, slowing for hazards and never impeding flow.

Signal meanings create a classic trap between go and wait. Green means go if clear, green arrow allows only the arrow direction after yielding, yellow warns red is near and flashing yellow means caution. Red means stop and wait, right on red comes after stop unless barred, flashing red is stop-then-go, and red arrows require waiting. An officer directing traffic overrides any signal, and a dead signal needs a stop-first treat as stop. Never rush a green without checking the path.

Signs and express payment complete the picture for daily driving. Guide signs inform, railroad crossings need caution and stop discipline, regulatory signs command, warning diamonds alert, and work zones are orange with doubled speeding fines and flagger obedience. For express lanes, single-occupant use needs a paid pass account, while a clean-fuel decal is a separate windshield authorization. Read the sign family first, then confirm whether you hold the correct authorization.

Here is a quick check: at a red light with an officer waving you through, must you stay stopped or follow the officer. Consider normal red discipline with right on red, red arrows and flashing red, then weigh the officer override rule. A dead signal also needs a stop-first approach. Choose the lawful action and explain why the higher authority controls.

lines.text: Four-way-stop tie yields to the right.

narration.text: Finish with priority discipline that protects every crossing. Assess safety instead of assuming priority. Yield to an earlier intersection arrival, to oncoming drivers when turning left, and to the driver on the right when both reach a four-way stop together. A driver leaving a driveway or private road yields to public-road traffic, and an entrance-ramp driver yields to traffic already on the interstate. Yield also to pedestrians, bicyclists and others remaining in the intersection. Carry that habit through signals, markings and lane choices. Courtesy and rule obedience make shared space more predictable.

why_how.text: Green still needs a clear path because cross traffic or walkers may remain inside, so go-if-clear prevents intersection crashes.
Officer override matters because live direction can respond to hazards that fixed signals cannot see.

reasoning.text: The driver sees green but cross traffic remains, and an officer then waves traffic to stop, so waiting obeys both rules.

result.text: The driver waits behind the line until the officer and intersection are clear.

scenario.text: A driver faces a green light while a late vehicle clears ahead and an officer steps in to direct traffic.
